query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the spray parameters on the HVAF‐i7 torch by increasing particle velocity—which can be effectively achieved by setting the nozzle-to-substrate distance to around 300–350 mm—will overcome the thickness limitation for FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coats. This increase in particle velocity enhances in‐flight particle melting, flattening, and subsequent inter‐splat bonding, leading to a thicker, well-adherent coating.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a 15–45 μm particle size; feedstock that previously yielded high-quality coatings on the HVAF-M3 system.
generation.intervention: Adjust HVAF-i7 deposition parameters to increase particle velocity, specifically by selecting a nozzle distance in the 300–350 mm range (as shown effective in conventional MCrAlY studies) while keeping the same 15–45 μm feedstock.
generation.conditions: Deposition on substrates (including those within internal diameters as small as 120 mm) under high-temperature thermal-barrier service conditions; similar substrate pre-treatment and environmental control as in baseline experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced in-flight kinetic energy leads to improved particle melting, flattening, and inter-splat bonding, resulting in a higher deposition efficiency and thicker, adherent coatings with minimal oxidation.
generation.mechanism: By increasing the particle velocity through an optimal spray distance, individual powder particles attain greater kinetic energy upon impact. This results in more effective splat formation and coalescence, which increases the coating build-up and deposition rate while the brief in-flight exposure minimizes the extent of oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (15–45 μm feedstock deposited by HVAF-i7 under non-optimized conditions), the intervention is expected to yield a significantly thicker bond coat that maintains coating integrity, exhibits low levels of as-sprayed oxidation, and retains durability during high-temperature service.
generation.baseline: High-quality, thin FeCoNiCrAl HEA coatings produced using 15–45 μm feedstock under standard HVAF-i7 parameters (inadequate thickness compared to HVAF-M3 results).
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is limited to similar feedstock properties and torch configurations; too high a particle velocity or overly long standoff distances might induce undesirable oxidation or incomplete melting, compromising coating quality.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in coating thickness and the balance between increased deposition rate and oxidation suppression require further calibration for the HVAF-i7 system.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled study in which FeCoNiCrAl HEA powder (15–45 μm) is deposited using the HVAF-i7 torch under two sets of conditions: (a) standard parameters (baseline) and (b) optimized parameters with a nozzle distance set to 300–350 mm (to increase particle velocity). Use substrates with internal diameters as small as 120 mm and simulate high-temperature thermal-barrier service.
measurements: Oxide content and phase composition (via XRD/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized HVAF-i7 conditions do not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness while maintaining comparable adhesion and low oxidation levels relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

To date, in addition to traditional casting and forging methods, various thermal spraying techniques have been employed to coat HEAs on the substrate, firstly, high-velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF) [,] technique in which a specially designed torch allows the compressed flame to expand freely consuming the gases combustion, such as Hydrocarbon’s, i.e., Methane (CH4), Propane (C3H6), Butane (C4H8) or kerosene oil type liquid fuels. O2 and fuel are mixed in the combustion zone under conditions that display the correct combustion mode and pressure []. This process generates a very high-velocity flame which is used to propel the particles at near-supersonic speeds before making an impact on the substrate [].
